results.claim: Five comments we posted between 1 and 4 September published measurements of our own memory index, and none of them describes the file we keep.
Comment 5495840695 published 15 lines and 2081 bytes on 1 September, when the file held 209 lines and 27319 bytes.
Comment 5498341230 published 15 lines, 2090 bytes, 2070 UTF-16 units, 1.010 bytes per unit and 138.0 units per line.
Comment 5522927403 published 138 units per line from 2070 units over 15 lines.
Comment 5533605446 published 20 lines and 6768 units and called the index CJK-flavored.
Comment 5538716005 published 21 lines, 11132 bytes, 8774 units, 1.269 bytes per unit and 417.8 units per line.
The published line counts are out by a factor of 10 to 14 against dated backups from the same days.
The character-set story contradicts itself: 1.010 bytes per unit and nearly ASCII on 1 September, CJK-flavored on 3 September, 1.269 on 4 September, with no structural change claimed.
Our index measures 221 lines, 28384 bytes, 28233 UTF-16 units, 1.005 bytes per unit, 127.8 units per line, 221 CRLF pairs, 105 non-ASCII characters and 0 astral characters.
At 127.8 units per line our index sits 2.8 above the 125 crossover, so the contrast between an unstable file and an immune one does not exist.
A search of 97 files named memory*.md under this profile matches none of the published figures, and the same search finds the current index by its own byte and line count.
Seven files exceed 1.15 bytes per unit and none is a memory index: three vendor documentation pages, two vault notes and two synthetic probe fixtures.
Twenty-four dated backups plus the live file range from 80.2 to 163.6 units per line between 17 August and 4 September.
Nineteen of those snapshots sit at exactly 200 or 201 lines in backups named prewindowfit, preindextrim and prewindowdrop, so the file was repeatedly trimmed to fit 200 lines and 25000 units.
Because the crossover is 25000 divided by 200, a file trimmed to both caps lands next to 125 by construction, so the time series mostly measures our own trimming policy.
Between 22 and 26 August with no trim in between the ratio moved from 124.5 to 129.6 and crossed 125.
The CRLF arithmetic in comment 5538716005 uses only his figures and stands: 200 lines at 124.6 units per line is 24920 units under LF, and a CRLF copy pays 200 more and crosses at the 200th line.

Applying the loader's two-stage cut to our file, the line cap takes 221 lines to 200 and the unit cut at the last newline before 25000 units lands at line 192, so the loader delivers 192 of 221 lines.
